title: Cooking 5 Meals You'll Actually Eat
summary: A small repeating menu beats endless variety. Pick five forgiving recipes with overlapping ingredients, prep once a week, and stop deciding what to cook every night.

sections.title: The Moment
sections.value: It's a Tuesday in week three. The fridge holds half a bag of spinach you bought with good intentions, three eggs, a wedge of cheese, and a sad-looking capsicum. The pantry has rice, pasta, a curry paste you opened once, and a tin of chickpeas. You're standing in front of all of it knowing you have everything you need to cook something — and absolutely no idea what that something is. So you order Uber Eats. Again. The receipt says $24 and you've done this three times this week.

sections.title: The Feeling
sections.value:
It's not laziness. Decision fatigue is real, and *what should I cook tonight* is one of the most expensive open questions you can leave to a tired version of yourself at 7pm. The recipe apps don't help — they give you 800 options and ask you to choose, which is the opposite of what your brain is short on.

What you actually need is fewer choices, not more inspiration.

sections.title: What nobody told you
sections.value:
You don't need recipes. You need a **system of five repeat meals** that share ingredients, take less than 30 minutes each, and forgive substitutions. Once they're locked in, weekday dinner stops being a decision and starts being a default.

The people you envy — the ones who seem to cook for themselves without drama — almost never have a wide repertoire. They have five things they can do half-asleep, and they rotate. That's the whole trick.

sections.title: How it actually works
sections.value:
**1. Pick five meals that overlap.**

The goal is a starter pantry of maybe fifteen ingredients that becomes five different dinners depending on how you combine them. A workable starter set:

- **One-pot pasta** — pasta, garlic, onion, tinned tomatoes, whatever vegetable is in the fridge, parmesan
- **Egg fried rice** — leftover rice, eggs, garlic, soy sauce, frozen peas, spring onion
- **Coconut chickpea curry** — onion, garlic, curry powder or paste, tinned chickpeas, coconut milk, frozen spinach, served on rice
- **Stir-fried noodles** — noodles, soy sauce, garlic, whatever protein, whatever vegetable
- **Loaded baked potato or sweet potato** — microwave 8 minutes, top with tinned tuna, cheese, beans, or leftover curry

Notice the overlap: garlic, onion, soy sauce, rice and frozen vegetables work in four out of five. ANU's student cooking guide makes the same point — *most recipes can handle a missing or swapped ingredient*. Treat recipes like templates, not instructions.

**2. Prep once, eat five times.**

Frugal & Thriving's meal-prep guide describes three approaches that all work: **freezer meals** (cook large batches of curry/stew/bolognese, freeze in single portions, lasts ~3 months), **portioned meals** (cook protein, starch and vegetable separately, mix in containers), and **fresh prep** (chop and marinate ahead so weeknight cooking is just heat-and-combine). Pick one — usually fresh prep on a Sunday afternoon, takes 60–90 minutes — and the rest of the week becomes assembly, not cooking.

**3. Build a base shop, not a meal-by-meal shop.**

The shopping list for those five meals is roughly:

- Pasta · rice · noodles · oats
- Eggs · cheese · milk
- One protein (chicken, mince, tofu, or canned tuna)
- Tinned tomatoes · tinned chickpeas · coconut milk
- Onion · garlic · ginger · soy sauce · curry paste · olive oil
- Frozen mixed vegetables · frozen spinach · frozen peas
- One or two fresh vegetables (capsicum, broccoli, whatever's on special)

That's roughly $45–$60 at ALDI and feeds one person for a week with leftovers. Frozen vegetables matter — they don't rot, they're often nutritionally identical to fresh, and they cut food waste, which is where most one-person grocery budgets quietly leak money.

**4. Optimise for tired-Tuesday-you, not aspirational-Sunday-you.**

Sunday-you wants to make a Thai green curry from scratch. Tuesday-you wants to eat something hot in fifteen minutes and go to bed. The five meals should be picked for Tuesday-you. If a recipe needs more than one pot, more than 30 minutes, or an ingredient you have to go out for, it doesn't belong on the list — at least not yet.

**5. Add new meals slowly, one at a time.**

Once the five are stable for a few weeks, swap one out for something new. That's it. You're not building a cookbook in your head — you're building a small, reliable rotation that quietly absorbs new things over months, not weeks.

### The bit nobody mentions

Most people who say they 'can't cook' aren't bad cooks. They've just never given themselves permission to eat the same thing twice in a week. The pressure to make every dinner novel is a cultural inheritance from food media, and it's the single biggest reason fridges full of ingredients become Uber Eats orders.

Five meals on rotation is not a failure of imagination. It's how almost everyone who feeds themselves well actually does it.
